n: Years have passed. Now Babylon’s army surrounds Jerusalem (about 588 BC), and King Zedekiah sends two officials to Jeremiah for a word from the Lord. Zedekiah was king when Lehi left Jerusalem.

f.g: Judah’s last king (about 597–586 BC), installed by Nebuchadnezzar.
Not the same Pashur as in chapter 20.

n: The king hopes for a miracle like the one in Hezekiah’s day, when the Lord drove the Assyrians away from Jerusalem overnight.

f.g: A spelling closer to the Babylonian Nabû-kudurri-uṣur; same king as Nebuchadnezzar.

f.w: according to all his wondrous works

n: Jeremiah gives the messengers a reply to carry back to the king.
The answer is the opposite of what Zedekiah hoped: the Lord will turn Judah’s weapons back on itself and drive the defenders inside the walls.

f.g: The people of southern Babylonia; the dynasty of Nebuchadnezzar was Chaldean, so the word often just means Babylonians.

n: Shockingly, God himself will fight against Jerusalem—using the same “outstretched hand” and “strong arm” language that once described him rescuing Israel from Egypt.

f.w: with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm

n: Disease will sweep through the crowded, besieged city, killing people and animals alike.
Survivors of plague, sword, and famine—including Zedekiah himself—will fall into Nebuchadnezzar’s hands, and he will show no mercy. This was fulfilled when Jerusalem fell.

f.w: I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah

n: Now a message to the people: God sets before them two paths—life and death. The words echo Moses’ great choice, but here “life” means surrender.

f.w: the way of life, and the way of death

n: Those who stay in the city will die; those who go out and surrender to the Babylonians will survive, escaping with their lives as their only “prize.” This counsel later got Jeremiah accused of treason.

f.w: his life shall be unto him for a prey
f.g: An idiom: he will escape with his life as his only plunder.

n: God has set his face against the city. It will be handed to Babylon and burned.
A separate message for the royal family follows.
The kings in David’s line must do justice “in the morning”—promptly and consistently—and rescue the robbed from oppressors, or God’s anger will burn like an unquenchable fire.

f.g: Kings often held court early in the day; justice should be the first order of business.
The one who has been robbed.

n: God addresses Jerusalem as a proud “rock” on a plateau surrounded by valleys, whose people boast that no enemy can get in.

f.w: inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain
f.g: Jerusalem sits on ridges ringed by valleys—naturally defensible, which bred false confidence.

n: But God will repay them according to what their deeds deserve, setting a fire in their “forest”—possibly a poetic name for the cedar-paneled palace buildings.
